not.** Everything computed on this page comes from the code chunks in it,
with parameter values chosen to resemble published models and stated where
they are chosen. The published estimates in Section 8 were transcribed from
the papers by a fetch tool and carry ⚠️ in [references.qmd](references.qmd);
the theory sources are from abstracts and carry ❌. The

## In brief

**The question.** A monoclonal antibody depletes circulating B cells. The
standard model is an indirect response with the drug raising the B-cell loss
rate through $E_{\max} C / (EC_{50} + C)$. Published fits of this model report
$E_{\max}$ near 150, and either report $EC_{50}$ with a wide interval, or fix
it, or give up on it and fit a slope instead. Is $EC_{50}$ estimable at all,
and if so from what?

**The answer.** ⚠️ **$EC_{50}$ is estimable only through $E_{\max}$, and
$E_{\max}$ is estimable only from the first days of depletion or from a cohort
held in a concentration band two orders of magnitude below $EC_{50}$. With a
first post-dose B-cell sample at a week and doses that deplete completely, the
two parameters are perfectly correlated and only their ratio is identified.**
Three quantities in the data carry three pieces of information: the recovery
tail carries $k_{\rm out}$; the speed of the initial fall carries
$k_{\rm out} E_{\max}$; the timing of the recovery's start carries
$E_{\max}/EC_{50}$. Lose the first days, and the second piece is gone, and
$E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ collapse onto one ridge. Section 2 derives each of
these from the model equation, Section 5 shows them in the sensitivities, and
Section 6 puts numbers on them by design.

**Why a large $E_{\max}$ makes it worse.** The nadir is $B_0/(1 + E)$. With
$E_{\max} = 150$, the count at $C = EC_{50}$ is already 1.3% of baseline,
below any flow-cytometry limit. Half-maximal *depletion* happens at
$C \approx EC_{50}/150$. The concentration band over which the cell count can
say anything about $EC_{50}$ separately from $E_{\max}$ is therefore far below
every therapeutic dose, and usually below the PK assay. Section 4.

**What to do instead.** Parameterize the drug effect as the slope
$S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$, which is what Schoemaker et al. proposed in 1998 for
exactly this situation and what the inebilizumab model did in 2022, and test
the $E_{\max}$ form only when a cohort has a quantifiable nadir. Section 9.
Everything downstream that depends on the duration of depletion depends on the
slope and $k_{\rm out}$, and loses nothing.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Recovery tail<br/>days 150 to 300"] --> K["k_out"]
    B["Speed of the fall<br/>days 0 to 3"] --> KE["k_out × Emax"]
    C["When recovery starts<br/>days 80 to 140"] --> R["Emax / EC50"]
    K --> KE
    KE --> E["Emax"]
    E --> R
    R --> EC["EC50"]
```

**Out of scope, stated once.**

- ❌ **Target-mediated drug disposition.** The PK here is linear. Where a
  published model ties the effect to receptor occupancy with a binding
  constant fixed from in vitro data, that is a different route to the same
  place and Section 8 notes it.
- ❌ **Tissue B cells.** Only the circulating count is modelled, because only
  it is measured.
- ❌ **Any recommendation about a named drug's dose.** The compounds in
  Section 8 are sources of parameter values and of what happened when the
  model was fit.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. The model

An indirect response model of the fourth Jusko type: the drug stimulates the
loss of the response variable. With $B$ the circulating B-cell count,

$$
\frac{dB}{dt} = k_{\rm in} - k_{\rm out}\,\big(1 + E(C)\big)\,B, \qquad
E(C) = \frac{E_{\max}\, C}{EC_{50} + C}, \qquad B(0) = B_0 = \frac{k_{\rm in}}{k_{\rm out}}
$$

and one-compartment PK after an intravenous bolus, $C(t) = (D/V) e^{-k_e t}$.

| Symbol | What it is | Value used here | Why that value |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| $B_0$ | Baseline B-cell count | 200 cells/µL | Typical adult; ofatumumab model 194, inebilizumab 135 |
| $k_{\rm out}$ | B-cell loss rate; sets the repopulation speed | 0.02 per day | Half-life 35 d; ofatumumab 0.0124/d, paediatric rituximab CD19 half-life 173 d |
| $E_{\max}$ | Maximum fold-increase in loss rate | 150 | Ofatumumab 159, paediatric rituximab 155 |
| $EC_{50}$ | Concentration for half of $E_{\max}$ | 1 mg/L | Arbitrary scale; only $C/EC_{50}$ enters |
| $V$, $CL$ | Volume, clearance | 3 L, 0.2 L/day | Half-life 10.4 d, an IgG1 antibody |
| LOQ | Flow-cytometry limit for B cells | 5 or 10 cells/µL | 2.5% or 5% of baseline |
| $\sigma$ | Proportional residual error | 30% | Inebilizumab model 61%, ofatumumab lower; 30% is generous to the design |

: Parameters of the simulated system {tbl-colwidths="[12,34,20,34]"}

The published values are in [references.qmd](references.qmd), entries 5 to 8,
transcribed and not verified.

```{r setup}
library(ggplot2); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(xgxr); library(rxode2)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(20260909); xgx_theme_set()
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.height = 4, fig.width = 6.5)
# Palette: the first three categorical slots of the reference palette in the
# dataviz skill, documented as validated for all pairs; a single-hue ramp for dose.
pal3 <- c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a")
ramp5 <- c("#c6dbef", "#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c")

Emax <- 150; EC50 <- 1; kout <- 0.02; B0 <- 200; V <- 3; CL <- 0.2

# The model: one-compartment PK after an IV bolus into A, and B cells made at
# kout * B0 and lost at kout * (1 + E(C)). slope = 1 swaps the Emax drug effect
# for the log-linear slope form used in Section 9.
bcell <- rxode2({
  C <- A / V
  if (slope == 1) {
    E <- S * log(1 + C / Cref)
  } else {
    E <- Emax * C / (EC50 + C)
  }
  d/dt(A) <- -CL / V * A
  B(0) <- B0
  d/dt(B) <- kout * B0 - kout * (1 + E) * B
})

# B-cell count at the requested times after a single dose. Tight tolerances,
# because Sections 5 and 6 take finite differences of the output.
sim_B <- function(dose, Emax, EC50, kout, B0 = 200, times,
                  form = "emax", S = 0, Cref = 1) {
  ev <- et(amt = dose, cmt = "A") %>% et(times)
  p <- c(Emax = Emax, EC50 = EC50, kout = kout, B0 = B0, V = V, CL = CL,
         slope = as.numeric(form == "slope"), S = S, Cref = Cref)
  out <- rxSolve(bcell, p, ev, atol = 1e-12, rtol = 1e-10, returnType = "data.frame")
  out$B[match(times, out$time)]
}
```

## 2. Which part of the curve carries which parameter

**After a single depleting dose, the B-cell curve has five parts, and each is
set by one parameter or one combination of parameters: the baseline by
$B_0$, the fall by $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$, the floor by $E_{\max}$, the
time the count climbs back by $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$, and the tail by
$k_{\rm out}$. No part is set by $EC_{50}$ alone.**

```{r feature-map, fig.height=7.5, fig.width=8, fig.cap="A: the model. B: the five parts of the B-cell curve after a dose with Cmax = 100 × EC50, numbered as in Sections 2.2 to 2.6; the dashed line is the limit of quantification at 5% of baseline. C: time for the count to climb back above 5% of baseline against peak concentration. Points are ODE solutions for four parameter sets; lines are the formula of Section 2.5, which depends on Emax/EC50 only. The three sets sharing Emax/EC50 = 150 fall on one line."}
f_loq <- 0.05; ke <- CL / V; S0 <- Emax / EC50

# A: the model, drawn
pA <- ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = c(0.7, 2.7), xmax = c(1.3, 3.3), ymin = 1.7, ymax = 2.3, fill = "grey88", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = c(1, 3), y = 2, label = c("C", "B"), size = 6) +
  annotate("segment", x = c(1, 1, 3, 3), xend = c(1, 1, 3, 3), y = c(3, 1.7, 3, 1.7), yend = c(2.3, 1, 2.3, 1),
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = c(1.08, 0.92, 3.08, 3.08), y = c(2.65, 1.35, 2.65, 1.35), hjust = c(0, 1, 0, 0), size = 3.2, parse = TRUE,
           label = c("Dose", "k[e] == CL/V", "k[out]*B[0]", "k[out]*(1 + E(C))")) +
  annotate("curve", x = 1.3, y = 1.85, xend = 2.95, yend = 1.3, linetype = 2, curvature = 0.25,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")), colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.9, y = 0.85, parse = TRUE, size = 3.2,
           label = "E(C) == frac(E[max]*C, EC[50] + C)") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 4.5), ylim = c(0.5, 3.1)) + theme_void() +
  labs(title = "A. Model")

# B: the five parts on one curve
d_short <- seq(0, 3, by = 0.01); d_long <- seq(0, 300, by = 1)
panels <- c("First 3 days", "Days 0 to 300")
cur <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(panel = panels[1], day = d_short, B = sim_B(300, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = d_short)),
  data.frame(panel = panels[2], day = d_long,  B = sim_B(300, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = d_long)))
cur$panel <- factor(cur$panel, levels = panels)
t_half_fall <- log(2) / (kout * (1 + Emax)); B_floor <- B0 / (1 + Emax)
t_f <- log(f_loq * S0 * 100 / (1 - f_loq)) / ke
pf <- function(x) factor(x, levels = panels)
labB <- data.frame(panel = pf(panels[c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2)]),
  day = c(0.12, t_half_fall + 0.12, 1.2, t_f + 8, 190), B = c(230, 100, B_floor * 0.7, 7, 120), hjust = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  lab = c('"1  baseline:"~B[0]', '"2  fall: rate"~k[out]*(1+E[max])', '"3  floor:"~B[0]/(1+E[max])',
          '"4  climb back:"~E[max]/EC[50]', '"5  tail: rate"~k[out]'))
pB <- ggplot(cur, aes(day, B)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = f_loq * B0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(data = data.frame(panel = pf(panels[1])), aes(yintercept = B_floor), linetype = 3, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = pal3[1]) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(panel = pf(panels), day = c(t_half_fall, t_f), B = c(B0 / 2, f_loq * B0)),
             size = 2.5, colour = pal3[2]) +
  geom_text(data = labB, aes(label = lab, hjust = hjust), parse = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100), limits = c(0.8, 300)) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "B cells per µL, log scale", title = "B. Five parts of the curve")

# C: climb-back time across doses, simulated and from the formula
t_climb <- function(dose, Emax, EC50) {
  tt <- seq(0, 600, by = 0.5); B <- sim_B(dose, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt)
  i <- which.min(B); if (B[i] >= f_loq * B0) return(NA)
  tt[i - 1 + which(B[i:length(B)] >= f_loq * B0)[1]]
}
sets <- data.frame(Emax = c(50, 150, 450, 150), EC50 = c(1/3, 1, 3, 10))
sets$set <- sprintf("Emax %g, EC50 %.2g", sets$Emax, sets$EC50)
sets$S0 <- sprintf("Emax/EC50 = %g", sets$Emax / sets$EC50)
cc <- 10^seq(-0.5, 3, by = 0.25)
climb <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(sets)), function(k)
  data.frame(sets[k, ], cmax = cc, t = sapply(cc * V, t_climb, Emax = sets$Emax[k], EC50 = sets$EC50[k]))))
climb$set <- factor(climb$set, levels = sets$set)
lines_C <- bind_rows(lapply(unique(sets$Emax / sets$EC50), function(s0)
  data.frame(S0 = sprintf("Emax/EC50 = %g", s0), cmax = cc, t = log(f_loq * s0 * cc / (1 - f_loq)) / ke))) %>%
  filter(t > 0)
pC <- ggplot(climb, aes(cmax, t, colour = S0)) +
  geom_line(data = lines_C, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = set), size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal3[1:2], name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16, 2, 15), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Cmax, mg/L, log scale", y = "Day the count climbs above 5%", title = "C. Dose escalation") +
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.text = element_text(size = 8))

(pA | pC) / pB + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.1))
```

| Part | When | Formula | Carries |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1. Baseline | before the dose, and long after | $B = B_0$ | $B_0$ |
| 2. Fall | first one to two days | $t_{1/2,\rm fall} \approx \dfrac{\ln 2}{k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})}$ | $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$ |
| 3. Floor | while $C \gg EC_{50}$ | $B \approx \dfrac{B_0}{1 + E_{\max}}$ | $E_{\max}$ |
| 4. Climb back | when $E(C)$ falls to $(1-f)/f$ | $t_f \approx \dfrac{1}{k_e} \ln \dfrac{f\, S_0\, C_{\max}}{1 - f}$ | $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$ |
| 5. Tail | once $S_0 C \ll 1$ | $B_0 - B \propto e^{-k_{\rm out} t}$ | $k_{\rm out}$ |
| Low dose | $C_{\max} \ll EC_{50}$ throughout | nadir depth $\approx S_0 C_{\max} (k_{\rm out}/k_e)^{k_e/(k_e - k_{\rm out})}$ | $S_0$, $k_{\rm out}$ |

: The five parts of the curve, with $f$ the fraction of baseline at which the count is read, here the 5% quantification limit {tbl-colwidths="[14,26,38,22]"}

### 2.1 Two rates decide the shape

Dividing the model equation of Section 1 by $B$ gives

$$
\frac{d \ln B}{dt} = k_{\rm out} \left( \frac{B_0}{B} - 1 - E(C) \right)
$$

At any fixed concentration this pulls $B$ toward its quasi-steady state
$B_{\rm qss} = B_0 / (1 + E(C))$, the level at which the bracket is zero,
at the rate $k_{\rm out}(1 + E(C))$. The concentration itself falls at the
rate $k_e = CL/V$. Which of the two rates is larger decides whether $B$ keeps
up with the drug:

- **$k_{\rm out}(1 + E) \gg k_e$**: $B$ follows $B_{\rm qss}$, and its level
  at any time is fixed by the concentration at that time.
- **$k_{\rm out}(1 + E) \ll k_e$**: $B$ lags the drug, and its return is
  limited by its own turnover.

The first rate changes by a factor of $1 + E_{\max}$ over the course of one
dose. With the values of Section 1 it is $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max}) = 3.0$ per
day at the start, 45 times $k_e = 0.067$ per day, and $k_{\rm out} = 0.02$ per
day at the end, 0.3 times $k_e$. The curve begins fast and ends slow, and that
ordering is why its parts separate.

Peletier, Gabrielsson and Haag (references, entry 15) put the same point in
dimensionless form: with time scaled by $1/k_e$ and the count by $B_0$, the
whole curve is fixed by three numbers, $\kappa = k_{\rm out}/k_e$,
$E_{\max}$, and $C_{\max}/EC_{50}$. The two rates above are $\kappa$ and
$\kappa(1 + E_{\max})$ in those units. Krzyzanski and Jusko (entry 17) show
the same competition for an infusion: the response approaches its steady
state at the slower of $k_e$ and $k_{\rm out}(1 + E)$. Sections 2.3 to 2.8
note where each result below is already in these papers. Several of them
originate in Krzyzanski and Jusko 1997 (entry 13), the bolus paper the others
build on. That paper has not been obtained, so it is cited here as given in
Sharma and Jusko 1996.

The model also depends on concentration only through $C/EC_{50}$, so scaling
the dose and $EC_{50}$ by the same factor leaves the curve unchanged. Sharma
and Jusko made the same observation for all four indirect-response models in
1996 (references, entry 12).

### 2.2 The baseline

$B(0) = B_0$, and $B \to B_0$ as the drug clears. The baseline carries $B_0$
and nothing else.

### 2.3 The fall

For the first days, $t \ll 1/k_e = 15$ days, the concentration has barely
moved from $C_{\max}$, so the coefficient in the model equation is constant
and the equation is linear:

$$
B(t) = B_{\rm ss} + (B_0 - B_{\rm ss})\, e^{-k_f t}, \qquad
k_f = k_{\rm out}\big(1 + E(C_{\max})\big), \qquad
B_{\rm ss} = \frac{B_0}{1 + E(C_{\max})}
$$

The initial slope of $\ln B$ is $-k_{\rm out} E(C_{\max})$, and the time to
fall to half of baseline is

$$
t_{1/2,\rm fall} = \frac{1}{k_f} \ln \frac{B_0 - B_{\rm ss}}{B_0/2 - B_{\rm ss}}
\approx \frac{\ln 2}{k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})}
\quad \text{for } C_{\max} \gg EC_{50},\ E_{\max} \gg 1
$$

**The fall carries the product $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$.** $EC_{50}$
enters it only through $E(C_{\max}) = E_{\max}/(1 + EC_{50}/C_{\max})$, a 1%
correction at $C_{\max} = 100 \times EC_{50}$. With the values here,
$t_{1/2,\rm fall}$ is 0.23 days, five and a half hours, and the fall is 99%
complete by day 1.5.

Both pieces are published. Sharma and Jusko 1996 (entry 12, their Eq. 26,
taken from Krzyzanski and Jusko 1997) give the large-dose initial slope as $-k_{\rm out} B_0 S_{\max}$, the slope
above in absolute units. Peletier et al. (entry 15, their Eq. 32) prove that
for every dose

$$
B(t) > \frac{B_0}{1 + E_{\max}} \left(1 + E_{\max}\, e^{-k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max}) t}\right)
$$

and that the curve converges to this bound as the dose grows. The bound is the
fall formula above with $E(C_{\max})$ replaced by $E_{\max}$.

### 2.4 The floor

After the fall, $k_f \gg k_e$ and $B$ tracks the quasi-steady state:

$$
B(t) \approx \frac{B_0}{1 + E\big(C(t)\big)} \approx \frac{B_0}{1 + E_{\max}}
\quad \text{while } C(t) \gg EC_{50}
$$

**The floor carries $E_{\max}$**, given $B_0$, and is the large-dose limit of
the nadir in Sharma and Jusko 1996 (entry 12, their Eq. 14, taken from
Krzyzanski and Jusko 1997). With
$E_{\max} = 150$ it is 1.3 cells/µL. A floor is quantifiable only if it sits above the limit
$f B_0$, which needs $E_{\max} < 1/f - 1$: below 19 for a limit at 5% of
baseline, below 39 for one at 2.5%.

### 2.5 The climb back

The count stays on the quasi-steady state as the drug clears, and crosses the
fraction $f$ of baseline when $E(C) = (1 - f)/f$. Solving the $E_{\max}$
function for that concentration,

$$
C_f = EC_{50}\, \frac{1 - f}{f E_{\max} - (1 - f)}
$$

and with $C(t) = C_{\max} e^{-k_e t}$ the crossing time is

$$
t_f = \frac{1}{k_e} \ln \frac{C_{\max}}{C_f}
= \underbrace{\frac{1}{k_e} \ln \frac{f\, S_0\, C_{\max}}{1 - f}}_{\text{depends on } S_0 \text{ only}}
+ \underbrace{\frac{1}{k_e} \ln\left(1 - \frac{1 - f}{f E_{\max}}\right)}_{\text{the only place } E_{\max} \text{ enters alone}}
$$

**The climb back carries $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$**, given $k_e$ from the PK.
The second term is the only information about $E_{\max}$ separately that
survives in the recovery. With $f = 0.05$ it is $-2.0$ days at
$E_{\max} = 150$, $-7.2$ days at 50 and $-0.6$ days at 450: a shift of a few
days in a crossing that happens around day 100, read through 30% residual
error from monthly samples. This term is why the designs of Section 6 with a
first sample at day 7 leave $E_{\max}$ at 90% to over 800% relative standard
error rather than at infinity.

Two conditions hold the formula together. The count must still be on the
quasi-steady state at the crossing, which needs $k_{\rm out}/f \gg k_e$, or
$f \ll k_{\rm out}/k_e = 0.3$; when it fails the count lags and the crossing
comes a few days later than the formula says. And the crossing concentration
must be below $EC_{50}$, which holds whenever $f E_{\max} \gg 1$.

Across a dose escalation, $\partial t_f / \partial \ln C_{\max} = 1/k_e$, so
each ten-fold step in dose delays the climb by $\ln 10 / k_e = 34.5$ days,
3.3 PK half-lives, whatever $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ are. This is the
dose-duration relation usually attributed to Levy in 1966 (references, entry
11; the paper has not been obtained, and the attribution rests on secondary
sources): the duration of an effect is linear in log dose, the slope gives
the elimination rate, and the line extrapolates to zero duration at a
threshold dose, here $C_{\max} = (1 - f)/(f S_0)$. As those sources describe
it, Levy's relation is for a direct effect with a threshold. The indirect-response model gives the same line because the count
follows the quasi-steady state, which is a direct function of concentration.
Panel C of the figure shows the line and the points falling on it, with the
lowest doses bending away where the count never reaches the quasi-steady
state.

Peletier et al. (entry 15, their Eqs. 42 to 44) prove the general form of
this. As the dose grows, the recovery part of the curve converges to a fixed
shape that translates in time by $\ln(C_{\max}/EC_{50})/k_e$, a travelling
wave. The crossing time $t_f$ is where that shape crosses $f$, worked out
under the quasi-steady state; the shape itself depends on $E_{\max}$ and
$\kappa$, which is where the correction term above comes from.

### 2.6 The tail

Once $S_0 C \ll 1$, the drug effect is negligible and the model is
$dB/dt = k_{\rm out}(B_0 - B)$, so

$$
B_0 - B(t) \propto e^{-k_{\rm out} t}
$$

**The tail carries $k_{\rm out}$.** This needs $k_{\rm out} < k_e$. If the
cells turned over faster than the drug cleared, the count would follow the
drug down to baseline and the tail would carry $k_e$ instead, the
indirect-response version of flip-flop kinetics. Here $k_{\rm out}/k_e = 0.3$.

### 2.7 Doses that stay below EC50

When $C_{\max} \ll EC_{50}$ the drug effect is in its linear range for the
whole curve,

$$
E(C) = \frac{S_0 C}{1 + C/EC_{50}} = S_0 C \left(1 - \frac{C}{EC_{50}} + \dots\right) \approx S_0 C
$$

and the model becomes $dB/dt = k_{\rm out} B_0 - k_{\rm out}(1 + S_0 C) B$,
which contains $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ only as their ratio. **The whole
curve of a low dose, nadir included, carries $S_0$ and $k_{\rm out}$**, with
a correction of relative size $C_{\max}/EC_{50}$. When the depletion is also
shallow, $S_0 C_{\max} \ll 1$, the depth $\varepsilon = 1 - B/B_0$ obeys
$d\varepsilon/dt \approx k_{\rm out}(S_0 C - \varepsilon)$, which has the
same solution as an oral one-compartment PK model:

$$
\varepsilon(t) = \frac{k_{\rm out}\, S_0 C_{\max}}{k_e - k_{\rm out}} \left(e^{-k_{\rm out} t} - e^{-k_e t}\right),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{\max} = S_0 C_{\max} \left(\frac{k_{\rm out}}{k_e}\right)^{k_e/(k_e - k_{\rm out})}
$$

at $t = \ln(k_e/k_{\rm out})/(k_e - k_{\rm out})$, day 26 here. The nadir
depth is proportional to $S_0 C_{\max}$, with a factor of 0.18 set by the two
rates. The same solution and nadir time are Eqs. 34 and 35 of Peletier et al.
(entry 15), for the linear drug effect.

### 2.8 The area between baseline and curve

The area between the baseline and the B-cell curve, $\int_0^\infty (B_0 - B)\,dt$,
is the summary Sharma and Jusko (entry 12, their Eq. 22) and Peletier et al.
(entry 15, their Eq. 49) give for large doses:

$$
\text{area} \sim \frac{B_0}{k_e} \frac{E_{\max}}{1 + E_{\max}} \ln\left(1 + \frac{C_{\max}}{EC_{50}}\right)
\quad \text{as } C_{\max} \to \infty
$$

Peletier et al. note that $E_{\max}$ can be read from the slope of the area
against log dose. **For a B-cell depleting agent the slope carries almost no
$E_{\max}$:** the factor $E_{\max}/(1 + E_{\max})$ is 0.98 at
$E_{\max} = 50$ and 0.993 at 150. The formula is also a leading-order
statement, and at practical doses the omitted constant is larger than the
term kept. The table compares it with the area measured on the ODE solution
for the three parameter sets of panel C that share $S_0 = 150$.

```{r area}
area_ode <- function(dose, Emax, EC50) {
  tt <- seq(0, 3000, by = 0.5); sum(B0 - sim_B(dose, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt)) * 0.5
}
area <- expand.grid(k = 1:3, cmax = c(1, 10, 100, 1000)) %>%
  mutate(Emax = sets$Emax[k], EC50 = sets$EC50[k],
         ode = mapply(function(c, e, ec) area_ode(c * V, e, ec), cmax, Emax, EC50),
         formula = B0 / ke * Emax / (1 + Emax) * log(1 + cmax / EC50)) %>%
  select(cmax, Emax, EC50, ode, formula)
knitr::kable(area, digits = c(0, 0, 2, 0, 0),
  col.names = c("Cmax, mg/L", "Emax", "EC50, mg/L", "Area on the ODE, cells·day/µL", "Large-dose formula"),
  caption = "Area between baseline and B-cell curve, from the ODE solution and from the large-dose formula, for three parameter sets with Emax/EC50 = 150")
```

The measured area moves by $B_0 \ln 10 / k_e$ per ten-fold dose, as the
formula's slope says, and at a given dose it is nearly the same for all three
sets: like the climb back, it follows $S_0$. The formula's level is low by a
factor that shrinks only logarithmically with dose. The omitted constant is
of order $(B_0/k_e)\ln E_{\max} + B_0/k_{\rm out}$, the extra time for the
drug to fall from $EC_{50}$ to $EC_{50}/E_{\max}$ plus the lag of the
recovery, and with $E_{\max} = 150$ and slow turnover both are large. The
area is computed over the whole curve, including the part below the limit,
so it is not an observable a B-cell study can use directly in any case.

### 2.9 Checking the formulas against the ODE solution

Each formula above is an approximation, and each can be checked by solving
the model and measuring the feature it predicts. Forty parameter sets drawn
at random, log-uniformly, with $E_{\max}$ from 30 to 1000, $EC_{50}$ from 0.1
to 10 mg/L, $k_{\rm out}$ from 0.005 to 0.04 per day, and the dose putting
$C_{\max}$ between 30 and 1000 times $EC_{50}$, or for the low-dose check
between 0.003 and 0.1 times $1/S_0$. The PK is held at Section 1's values.

```{r feature-check, fig.height=5, fig.width=8, fig.cap="Each feature measured on the ODE solution against the formula of Sections 2.3 to 2.7, for forty random parameter sets. The line is identity. Fall: time to half of baseline. Floor: minimum count. Climb back: day the count rises above 5% of baseline. Tail: decay rate of B0 − B, fitted once S0·C < 0.001. Low dose: nadir depth as a fraction of baseline."}
set.seed(2)
n_chk <- 40
ps <- data.frame(Emax = exp(runif(n_chk, log(30), log(1000))), EC50 = exp(runif(n_chk, log(0.1), log(10))),
                 kout = exp(runif(n_chk, log(0.005), log(0.04))), r = exp(runif(n_chk, log(30), log(1000))),
                 r_low = exp(runif(n_chk, log(0.003), log(0.1))))
chk <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(n_chk), function(i) with(ps[i, ], {
  s0 <- Emax / EC50; cmax <- r * EC50
  tf <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.002); Bf <- sim_B(cmax * V, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tf)
  tt <- seq(0, 1500, by = 0.25); B <- sim_B(cmax * V, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt)
  i0 <- which.min(B)
  t1 <- log(s0 * cmax / 1e-3) / ke; w <- tt >= t1 & tt <= t1 + 60
  c_low <- r_low / s0; B_low <- sim_B(c_low * V, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = seq(0, 600, by = 0.25))
  data.frame(feature = c("Fall, days", "Floor, cells/µL", "Climb back, day", "Tail rate, per day", "Low-dose nadir depth"),
    ode = c(tf[which(Bf <= B0 / 2)[1]], min(B), tt[i0 - 1 + which(B[i0:length(B)] >= f_loq * B0)[1]],
            -unname(coef(lm(log(B0 - B[w]) ~ tt[w]))[2]), 1 - min(B_low) / B0),
    formula = c(log(2) / (kout * (1 + Emax)), B0 / (1 + Emax), log(f_loq * s0 * cmax / (1 - f_loq)) / ke,
                kout, s0 * c_low * (kout / ke)^(ke / (ke - kout))))
})))
chk$feature <- factor(chk$feature, levels = unique(chk$feature))
ggplot(chk, aes(formula, ode)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(colour = pal3[1], size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free", nrow = 2) +
  labs(x = "Formula", y = "Measured on the ODE solution")
```

```{r feature-check-table}
chk %>% group_by(feature) %>%
  summarise(median_err = median(100 * abs(ode / formula - 1)), max_err = max(100 * abs(ode / formula - 1)),
            max_days = if (grepl("day", first(feature))) max(abs(ode - formula)) else NA) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, col.names = c("Feature", "Median error, %", "Largest error, %", "Largest error, days"),
    caption = "Agreement between the formulas and the ODE solution over the forty parameter sets")
```

The fall and floor formulas err most where $C_{\max}$ is only 30 times
$EC_{50}$ or $k_{\rm out}$ is small, because the concentration has moved
before the fall is over and the floor is then $B_0/(1 + E(C))$ at a $C$ below
$C_{\max}$. The climb-back formula errs by days where $k_{\rm out}/f$ is not
much larger than $k_e$, the lag of Section 2.5. The tail and low-dose
formulas are close to exact.

### 2.10 What is identifiable and what is not

**Structurally, the model is identifiable**: with noise-free observations at
every time, the floor gives $E_{\max}$ and the fall gives it again, and
$EC_{50} = E_{\max}/S_0$ follows. Janzén et al. (references, entry 16)
checked a family of turnover and receptor-binding models formally and found
the same, with the same failure in practice: when the effect saturates, the
two parameters of the saturating function are estimated with high
uncertainty and correlation, and the ratio is estimated well. **The loss of
identifiability here is practical**, made by the quantification limit and
the sampling schedule, and the parts of Section 2.2 to 2.7 say exactly which
samples remove which parameter.

The identification chain itself is in Sharma and Jusko 1998 (entry 4, their
Table 1), as a graphical recipe: read the baseline, the initial slope and the
large-dose nadir; the nadir gives $S_{\max}$, the slope with $S_{\max}$ gives
$k_{\rm in}$ and so $k_{\rm out}$, and the concentration at the time of the
nadir gives $SC_{50}$. The design they say it needs is two or more bolus
doses, one high enough for full stimulation, and the baseline. For B cells the
first two readings are the ones a study loses: the nadir sits below the limit,
and the initial slope is over before a weekly sample.

| Part of the curve | Carries | Observed when | Usual B-cell study |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Baseline | $B_0$ | always | ✅ |
| Fall | $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$ | samples in the first one to two days, above the limit | ❌ first sample at a week |
| Floor | $E_{\max}$ | $E_{\max} < 1/f - 1$ | ❌ below the limit |
| Climb back | $S_0$; $E_{\max}$ only through a few-day correction | samples through recovery; $k_e$ from PK | ✅ |
| Tail | $k_{\rm out}$ | samples until repopulation | ✅ |
| Low-dose cohort | $S_0$, $k_{\rm out}$ | any dose with $C_{\max} \ll EC_{50}$ | ✅ when present, and adds no $E_{\max}$ |

: Which parameter each part of the curve identifies, and whether a typical study sees it

- ✅ **Identified by any design that follows the recovery to the end:** $B_0$,
  $k_{\rm out}$, and $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$.
- ⚠️ **$E_{\max}$: only from samples during the fall, or from a floor above
  the limit.** Without either, it is left with the climb-back correction of
  Section 2.5, a few days on a hundred-day timing.
- ❌ **$EC_{50}$ on its own: from no part of the curve.** It is identified
  exactly when $E_{\max}$ is, as $E_{\max}/S_0$, and with the same precision
  or worse.

The figure below makes the table concrete. Three parameter sets share
$S_0 = 150$ and differ three-fold in $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$. Above the
limit, their curves separate in the first two days and nowhere else.

```{r same-slope, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, fig.cap="B-cell count after the top dose for three parameter sets with the same Emax/EC50 = 150. The dashed line is the 5%-of-baseline limit. The curves differ above the limit only during the fall; their floors differ but are all below the limit, and their recoveries differ by a few days."}
same <- bind_rows(lapply(1:3, function(k) bind_rows(
  data.frame(set = sets$set[k], panel = panels[1], day = d_short,
             B = sim_B(300, sets$Emax[k], sets$EC50[k], kout, B0, times = d_short)),
  data.frame(set = sets$set[k], panel = panels[2], day = d_long,
             B = sim_B(300, sets$Emax[k], sets$EC50[k], kout, B0, times = d_long)))))
same$panel <- factor(same$panel, levels = panels); same$set <- factor(same$set, levels = sets$set[1:3])
ggplot(same, aes(day, B, colour = set)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = f_loq * B0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal3, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100), limits = c(0.3, 300)) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "B cells per µL, log scale") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## 3. What the data look like

Five single doses a ten-fold apart, the highest giving a peak concentration of
100 × $EC_{50}$ and the lowest 0.01 × $EC_{50}$. The horizontal line is a
flow-cytometry limit of 10 cells/µL.

```{r profiles, fig.cap="Simulated circulating B-cell count after single doses spanning four orders of magnitude in peak concentration. Every dose at or above 1 × EC50 depletes below the limit of quantification; the doses differ in how long they stay there."}
tt <- seq(0, 336, by = 2)
doses <- c(0.03, 0.3, 3, 30, 300)
prof <- bind_rows(lapply(doses, function(d)
  data.frame(dose = d, cmax = d / V, day = tt, B = sim_B(d, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt))))
prof$label <- factor(sprintf("%g", prof$cmax), levels = sprintf("%g", doses / V))
ggplot(prof, aes(day, B, colour = label)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ramp5, name = "Cmax, multiples of EC50") +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100), limits = c(0.5, 300)) +
  annotate("text", x = 330, y = 10, label = "LOQ", hjust = 1, vjust = -0.4, size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "B cells per µL, log scale") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Two things to read off. Between $C_{\max} = 1 \times EC_{50}$ and
$100 \times EC_{50}$ the curves are indistinguishable for the first two
months: same fall, same floor, all below the limit. What differs is when
recovery starts, and it starts later by $\ln 10/k_e = 34.5$ days, 3.3 PK
half-lives, for each ten-fold increase in dose (Section 2.5). And the only
curve that stays quantifiable throughout is the lowest, at $C_{\max} = 0.01 \times EC_{50}$, where the drug
effect is in its linear range and says nothing about $EC_{50}$ on its own.

## 4. The arithmetic of a large Emax

At a steady concentration $C$, the count settles at

$$
\frac{B_{ss}}{B_0} = \frac{1}{1 + E(C)} = \frac{1}{1 + E_{\max} C/(EC_{50} + C)}
$$

so that half-maximal depletion, $B_{ss} = B_0/2$, needs $E = 1$, which is at

$$
C_{1/2} = \frac{EC_{50}}{E_{\max} - 1}
$$

For $E_{\max} = 150$ that is $EC_{50}/149$. The concentration that halves the
drug's *effect on the rate* and the concentration that halves the *cell
count* are two orders of magnitude apart.

```{r depletion-curve, fig.cap="Steady-state depletion against concentration for three values of Emax. The vertical line is EC50. With Emax = 150, the whole descent from baseline to the quantification limit happens below EC50, and at EC50 itself the count is already at 1.3% of baseline."}
cc <- 10^seq(-4, 2, length.out = 300)
dep <- bind_rows(lapply(c(1, 10, 150), function(em)
  data.frame(Emax = em, C = cc, frac = 1 / (1 + em * cc / (1 + cc)))))
dep$Emax <- factor(paste("Emax =", dep$Emax), levels = paste("Emax =", c(1, 10, 150)))
ggplot(dep, aes(C, 100 * frac, colour = Emax)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, linetype = 3, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal3, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = 10^(-4:2), labels = c("0.0001", "0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1", "10", "100")) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 95, label = "EC50", hjust = -0.1, size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 1e-4, y = 5, label = "5% LOQ", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.4, size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Concentration, multiples of EC50, log scale", y = "Steady-state B cells, % of baseline") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The consequence is a band. Below $C_{1/2}/10$ the effect is small and linear
in $C$ with slope $E_{\max}/EC_{50}$. Above $EC_{50}$ the count is below the
limit whatever $C$ is. In between, the count is quantifiable and its level
depends on $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ separately. That band, roughly
$EC_{50}/1500$ to $EC_{50}/15$ here, is where a cohort would have to sit for
the nadir to identify the two parameters, and no therapeutic dose sits there.
Krzyzanski and Jusko made the same point for infusions in 1998 (references,
entry 17): two steady states give $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ only if their
concentrations are not both well above $EC_{50}$.

## 5. Where the information lives

The sensitivity of the log count to each log parameter, along the top-dose
profile, says what each observation can tell the estimator.

```{r sens, fig.cap="Sensitivity of log B-cell count to log Emax, log EC50 and log k_out over time after a dose with Cmax = 100 × EC50. Shaded region: count below a 5%-of-baseline limit, where no observation exists."}
tt <- seq(0, 336, by = 1); h <- 1e-4
f0 <- sim_B(300, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt)
sens <- data.frame(day = tt,
  Emax = (log(sim_B(300, Emax * exp(h), EC50, kout, B0, times = tt)) - log(f0)) / h,
  EC50 = (log(sim_B(300, Emax, EC50 * exp(h), kout, B0, times = tt)) - log(f0)) / h,
  kout = (log(sim_B(300, Emax, EC50, kout * exp(h), B0, times = tt)) - log(f0)) / h,
  B = f0)
blq <- range(sens$day[sens$B < 0.05 * B0])
sl <- pivot_longer(sens, c(Emax, EC50, kout), names_to = "parameter", values_to = "s")
sl$parameter <- factor(sl$parameter, levels = c("Emax", "EC50", "kout"))
ggplot(sl, aes(day, s, colour = parameter)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = blq[1], xmax = blq[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08, fill = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal3, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "d log B / d log parameter") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Three regions, and each one identifies one thing.

**Days 0 to 3, the fall.** Sensitivity to $E_{\max}$ and to $k_{\rm out}$ are
both large and equal, and sensitivity to $EC_{50}$ is near zero. At high
concentration the loss rate is $k_{\rm out}(1 + E_{\max})$, so the speed of the
fall identifies the product $k_{\rm out} E_{\max}$ and nothing about
$EC_{50}$. This is the only place $E_{\max}$ appears without $EC_{50}$ beside
it.

**Days 4 to 80, the floor.** Everything is below the limit. No observations,
no information.

**Days 80 to 200, the recovery.** Sensitivity to $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$
are equal and opposite: raising one or lowering the other shifts the curve
the same way. Recovery begins when $E(C)$ falls to order 1, which happens at
$C \approx EC_{50}/E_{\max}$, so this region identifies the ratio and only the
ratio. Sensitivity to $k_{\rm out}$ rises through the recovery and is the
last thing standing at day 250, so the tail identifies $k_{\rm out}$ alone.

The chain in the In brief diagram follows. $k_{\rm out}$ from the tail;
$k_{\rm out} E_{\max}$ from the fall, hence $E_{\max}$; $E_{\max}/EC_{50}$
from the recovery's timing, hence $EC_{50}$. Remove the fall from the data
and the chain breaks at its second link.

## 6. Expected precision by design

The Fisher information for the four log-parameters, from the sensitivities at
each sampling time, summed over patients and dose levels, with observations
below the limit dropped. Dropping them understates the information slightly,
since a censored value still says the count is below the limit, and the
comparison between designs is unaffected. Four dose designs, two limits, and
two sampling schedules that differ only in whether days 1 and 3 are sampled.

```{r fim}
t_dense  <- c(0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 56, 84, 112, 140, 168, 224, 280, 336)
t_sparse <- c(0, 7, 14, 28, 56, 84, 112, 140, 168, 224, 280, 336)
fim_design <- function(doses_n, loq, sigma = 0.3, times) {
  th <- log(c(Emax, EC50, kout, B0)); J <- NULL
  for (k in seq_along(doses_n$dose)) {
    d <- doses_n$dose[k]; n <- doses_n$n[k]
    f0 <- sim_B(d, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = times); keep <- f0 >= loq
    Jd <- sapply(1:4, function(j) { h <- 1e-4; th2 <- th; th2[j] <- th2[j] + h; p <- exp(th2)
      (log(sim_B(d, p[1], p[2], p[3], p[4], times = times)) - log(f0)) / h })
    J <- rbind(J, sqrt(n) * Jd[keep, , drop = FALSE])
  }
  Fi <- t(J) %*% J / sigma^2
  Vm <- tryCatch(solve(Fi), error = function(e) matrix(NA, 4, 4))
  se <- sqrt(diag(Vm))
  data.frame(rse_Emax = 100 * se[1], rse_EC50 = 100 * se[2],
             corr = Vm[1, 2] / sqrt(Vm[1, 1] * Vm[2, 2]),
             rse_slope = 100 * sqrt(Vm[1, 1] + Vm[2, 2] - 2 * Vm[1, 2]),
             rse_kout = 100 * se[3], n_obs = nrow(J))
}
designs <- list(
  "A: 300 mg only, 6 patients"                 = data.frame(dose = 300, n = 6),
  "B: 30, 100, 300 mg; 4 each"                 = data.frame(dose = c(30, 100, 300), n = 4),
  "C: 3 to 300 mg, five levels; 4 each"        = data.frame(dose = c(3, 10, 30, 100, 300), n = 4),
  "D: C with 0.03 and 0.3 mg replacing 10, 100" = data.frame(dose = c(0.03, 0.3, 3, 30, 300), n = 4))
grid <- expand.grid(design = names(designs), loq = c(5, 10), sampling = c("first sample day 1", "first sample day 7"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  tt <- if (grid$sampling[i] == "first sample day 1") t_dense else t_sparse
  cbind(grid[i, ], fim_design(designs[[grid$design[i]]], loq = grid$loq[i], times = tt))
}))
res %>% filter(loq == 5) %>% select(sampling, design, rse_Emax, rse_EC50, corr, rse_slope, rse_kout, n_obs) %>%
  arrange(sampling, design) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0),
    col.names = c("Sampling", "Design", "RSE Emax %", "RSE EC50 %", "corr(Emax, EC50)", "RSE Emax/EC50 %", "RSE k_out %", "Observations kept"),
    caption = "Expected precision from the Fisher information, LOQ 5 cells/µL (2.5% of baseline), 30% proportional error")
```

Read down the right-hand columns first. **The slope $E_{\max}/EC_{50}$ and
$k_{\rm out}$ are estimated in every design**, at a precision that improves
with cohorts and does not depend much on the early samples. Then read
$E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ against the sampling column. With days 1 and 3
sampled they are estimable, at 40 to 55% RSE from six patients at one dose
and around 10% from five cohorts. With the first sample at day 7 they are not
estimable in any design: the correlation is 1.00 and the RSEs run from about
90% to over 800%. Design D, which puts two cohorts at concentrations where the nadir
is quantifiable, does not rescue them, because those cohorts sit in the
linear range below the band of Section 4 and inform the slope, not its
factors.

```{r fim-loq}
res %>% filter(sampling == "first sample day 1") %>% select(loq, design, rse_Emax, rse_EC50, corr) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = loq, values_from = c(rse_Emax, rse_EC50, corr), names_glue = "{.value}, LOQ {loq}") %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2),
    caption = "The same, with days 1 and 3 sampled, at two quantification limits: the early samples do more than the limit")
```

## 7. The likelihood ridge

The Fisher information is a local statement. The shape of the objective
function over $(E_{\max}, EC_{50})$ with $k_{\rm out}$ and $B_0$ held at truth
shows the same thing globally. Design A, one simulated dataset per panel,
sparse sampling on the left and dense on the right.

```{r ridge, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, fig.cap="Sum of squared log-residuals over a grid of Emax and EC50 for one simulated six-patient dataset at the top dose. Left: first sample at day 7; the minimum is a ridge along Emax / EC50 = constant and any point on it fits equally well. Right: days 1 and 3 sampled; the ridge closes to a basin around the truth (cross)."}
sse_grid <- function(times, loq = 5, n = 6, seed = 7) {
  set.seed(seed)
  obs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:n, function(i) {
    f0 <- sim_B(300, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = times)
    y <- f0 * exp(rnorm(length(f0), 0, 0.3)); data.frame(t = times, y = y)[y >= loq & f0 >= loq, ]
  }))
  em <- 10^seq(0.5, 3.5, length.out = 41); ec <- 10^seq(-2, 2, length.out = 41)
  g <- expand.grid(Emax = em, EC50 = ec)
  g$sse <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(g)), function(i) {
    pred <- sim_B(300, g$Emax[i], g$EC50[i], kout, B0, times = times)
    sum((log(obs$y) - log(pred[match(obs$t, times)]))^2)
  })
  g
}
g1 <- sse_grid(t_sparse); g1$panel <- "First sample day 7"
g2 <- sse_grid(t_dense);  g2$panel <- "Days 1 and 3 sampled"
gg <- bind_rows(g1, g2) %>% group_by(panel) %>% mutate(d = sse - min(sse)) %>% ungroup()
gg$panel <- factor(gg$panel, levels = c("First sample day 7", "Days 1 and 3 sampled"))
ggplot(gg, aes(EC50, Emax)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = pmin(d, 40))) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = d), breaks = c(2, 6, 12), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("point", x = EC50, y = Emax, shape = 4, size = 3, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#08519c", high = "#f0f4fa", name = "SSE above\nminimum") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(x = "EC50, mg/L, log scale", y = "Emax, log scale")
```

The ridge on the left is the line $\log E_{\max} - \log EC_{50} =$ constant.
Any fitting algorithm started on it stays on it, reports a converged
$E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ with enormous standard errors or none, and gives the
right predictions inside the studied concentration range. That is the
situation Dutta et al. described in 1996 for the sigmoid $E_{\max}$ model
with truncated data (references, entry 2): the fit is good, the descriptors
inside the data are precise, and $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ are not.

## 8. What the published models found

| Drug, entry | Patients, doses | Drug effect form | What happened to $EC_{50}$ | Reference |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Ofatumumab, 5 | 1,486; 3 to 700 mg across five studies, including 3 and 10 mg arms with partial depletion | Sigmoid $E_{\max}$ on lysis, within TMDD; $K_D$ and $k_{\rm off}$ fixed from preclinical data | Estimated: 0.0057 mg/L, RSE 8.5%; $E_{\max}$ 159, RSE 3.2% | Yu et al., *CNS Drugs* 2022, [doi](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40263-021-00895-w) |
| Rituximab, paediatric, 6 | 63; full dose; 281 CD19 counts, 52% below the limit | $E_{\max}$ on degradation, driven by amount | Estimated: $ED_{50}$ 0.69 mg, RSE 61%, CI 0.18 to 2.26; $E_{\max}$ 155, CI 153 to 713; authors cite "the highly efficacious doses" | *Pharmaceutics* 2023;15:2534, [doi](https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics15112534) |
| Inebilizumab, 7 | 213; 0.1 to 10 mg/kg and 30 to 600 mg, a 100-fold range | Log-linear slope on removal | Abandoned: "the estimated EC50 ... was less than the assay lower limit of quantitation" | Yan et al., *Br J Clin Pharmacol* 2022, [doi](https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.15332) |
| Rituximab, membranous nephropathy, 8 | 41; 375 mg/m² × 4, 1000 mg × 2, 100 mg monthly | TMDD; elimination of the drug-CD20 complex | No $EC_{50}$; binding constant $k_{ss}$ at 60% RSE | [PMC11002205](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11002205/) |
| Ianalumab, Sjögren's, 9 | Phase 2 and RA data; 3 and 10 mg/kg single doses in the Phase 2 | Indirect-effect turnover; parameters not public | Not reported; a tissue receptor-occupancy model was added to carry the dose decision | Baltcheva et al., PAGE 2018, [abstract](https://www.page-meeting.org/Abstracts/model-based-dose-selection-for-the-phase-2b-study-of-ianalumab-in-primary-sjogrens-syndrome/) |

: Published indirect-response models of B-cell depletion and their $EC_{50}$ {tbl-colwidths="[16,22,20,24,18]"}

Three of the five read directly against Sections 5 and 6. Ofatumumab is the
case with cohorts in the band: the 3 mg and 10 mg subcutaneous arms gave
partial and delayed depletion, subcutaneous absorption slows the fall so that
weekly samples see it, and 1,486 patients did the rest. Rituximab at full dose
is the ridge, with a 13-fold interval on $ED_{50}$ and an upper bound on
$E_{\max}$ four times the estimate. Inebilizumab is the ridge recognized and
dealt with: the estimator put $EC_{50}$ below the PK assay, which is where
Section 4 says the band is, and the authors fit the slope instead.

Two of the five took the route around the problem: fix the binding constant
from in vitro measurements and let the model's potency come from the
literature rather than the data. That is a legitimate answer to "what is
$EC_{50}$", and it is not an estimate.

## 9. The slope parameterization

Schoemaker, van Gerven and Cohen showed in 1998 that when the data do not
approach $E_{\max}$, the parameter $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$, the initial slope
of the $E_{\max}$ curve, is estimable with good precision while its two
factors are not, and proposed reporting it (references, entry 1). The
inebilizumab model's $k = \text{slope} \cdot \log C$ is the same idea in a
form that stays finite at high concentration.

For everything downstream of the B-cell count, the slope is enough. The
duration of depletion, the time to repopulate to a fraction of baseline,
depends on when $E(C)$ falls to order 1, which is at $C \approx 1/S_0$, and
on $k_{\rm out}$. Fitting the slope model and the $E_{\max}$ model to the same
sparse data and predicting the duration across the studied dose range:

```{r trep, fig.cap="Time to repopulate to 20% of baseline against dose, from the true Emax model and from a log-linear slope model with its slope matched to the true initial slope. Inside the studied range the two agree; they part only below the lowest dose, where the slope model has no data to be wrong about."}
trep <- function(dose, form = "emax", S = 0, Cref = 1) {
  tt <- seq(0, 500, by = 1)
  B <- sim_B(dose, Emax, EC50, kout, B0, times = tt, form = form, S = S, Cref = Cref)
  i <- which.min(B); j <- which(B[i:length(B)] >= 0.2 * B0)[1]; if (is.na(j)) NA else tt[i + j - 1]
}
Cref <- 0.1
S_match <- Emax / EC50 * Cref     # equal initial slope: S/Cref = Emax/EC50
dd <- 10^seq(-1.5, 2.5, length.out = 17)
tr <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(model = "Emax, EC50 (true)", dose = dd, trep = sapply(dd, trep)),
  data.frame(model = "Log-linear slope",  dose = dd, trep = sapply(dd, trep, form = "slope", S = S_match, Cref = Cref)))
ggplot(tr, aes(dose, trep, colour = model)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 3, xmax = 300, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08, fill = "grey30") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal3[1:2], name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  annotate("text", x = 30, y = 20, label = "studied dose range", size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Dose, mg, log scale", y = "Days to repopulate to 20% of baseline") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## 10. What a study needs if it wants EC50

Stated as requirements, in the order they would be dropped from a protocol.

1. **B-cell samples on days 1 and 3 after the first dose.** The speed of the
   fall is the only observation that separates $E_{\max}$ from $EC_{50}$ at a
   therapeutic dose. With antibody-dependent lysis the fall is hours to days,
   and a first sample at a week arrives after it.
2. **B cells monthly until repopulation is complete in most patients.** The
   tail identifies $k_{\rm out}$, and without $k_{\rm out}$ the fall identifies
   nothing.
3. **A PK assay whose limit is below $EC_{50}/E_{\max}$**, or a willingness to
   extrapolate the PK tail by a factor of a hundred and say so. Recovery
   starts at concentrations the assay may never see.
4. **A cohort at a dose whose nadir is quantifiable and whose concentration
   sits inside the band of Section 4**, if the design can afford one. This is
   what ofatumumab had. A cohort below the band informs the slope and not the
   factors; a cohort above it is censored.
5. **Failing 1 and 4, fit the slope.** Report $S_0$ with its interval, state
   that $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ are identified as a ratio, and let anyone who
   needs the factors fix one of them from in vitro binding.

## 11. What this means for the ITP project

Section 6.2 of the
[ITP-PK-Platelet specification](../imm-itp-pk-platelet/specification.qmd) fits a
B-cell layer to a dose escalation of three to six patients per level, first
sample at a week, in order to carry the duration of depletion forward to a
platelet model. Sections 5 and 6 here say that design identifies the slope
and $k_{\rm out}$ at a usable precision and identifies neither $E_{\max}$ nor
$EC_{50}$; that Section 8 of the specification is right to parameterize by
the slope; and that if the escalation protocol can add days 1 and 3, the
$E_{\max}$ form becomes fittable at about 10% RSE across five cohorts, at the
cost of two blood draws.

## 12. Open questions

- **Sigmoidicity.** A Hill coefficient above 1 sharpens the band of Section 4
  and makes the recovery start more abruptly. Whether it is identifiable
  alongside the slope at these designs has not been checked.
- **Subcutaneous dosing.** Absorption over days slows the fall and moves the
  information of Section 5's first region into the first week, which is
  presumably part of why ofatumumab's model could see it. The simulations here
  are intravenous.
- **Censoring handled properly.** Dropping observations below the limit
  throws away the statement that they are below it. A likelihood with
  censored terms would recover some information at the floor, and the
  comparison between designs is not expected to change.
- **Between-patient variability.** The Fisher information here is for a
  population with fixed parameters. With 50 to 126% CV on the recovery rate in
  published models, the precision numbers in Section 6 are optimistic by a
  factor that a population-design tool would give.
